what: Radian is one of the largest private mortgage insurers in the United States. It protects lenders against losses when borrowers who put down less than 20% default, and it has been expanding into specialty insurance through the acquisition of Inigo, a Lloyd’s of London underwriter.
customers: Mortgage lenders and banks whose borrowers have small down payments, ultimately covering loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac; and, through Inigo, commercial insurance buyers in specialty lines.
money: Premiums on insurance protecting lenders against default on low-down-payment home loans.
Lloyd’s specialty underwriting through Inigo and investment income.
moat: An oligopoly: six private mortgage insurers share the US market, each approved by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac under strict capital rules that keep new entrants out.
risks: A sharp fall in house prices with rising unemployment would raise claims quickly.
Moving into Lloyd’s specialty insurance adds a business with different, catastrophe-exposed risks.
Housing reform affecting Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could change demand for private mortgage insurance.
opportunities: Large embedded home-price gains on insured loans make current claims very low.
Strong capital and cash generation support buybacks and dividends.
watch: The default rate on its insured portfolio and how many defaults turn into claims. Both are at historically low levels; any sustained rise is the first warning.
view: Mortgage insurers have been among the best-performing financial businesses since 2012, and Radian at about 9 times earnings is still priced as if the next housing crisis were around the corner. The reason claims are so low is that house prices rose sharply over the last decade: a borrower who defaults today usually has enough equity for the home to be sold without a loss. That cushion is the core of the investment case, and it makes the current earnings more durable than the cyclical reputation suggests.

Revenue jumped from about $1.2 billion in 2025 to $2.0 billion over the last twelve months because Radian bought Inigo, a specialty insurer at Lloyd’s. That deal is the debate. Management’s argument is diversification away from a single US housing risk; the counter-argument is that a well-run mortgage insurer has taken on a business with catastrophe and casualty exposure it has never managed. The price-to-free-cash-flow of 3.3 should not be relied on during this transition.

I think the core mortgage insurance franchise justifies more than 9 times earnings, but the acquisition adds uncertainty that may keep the multiple low for a while. Investors who want pure exposure to the mortgage insurance oligopoly may prefer peers that stayed focused; those who trust management’s capital allocation get a cheap entry. On balance the shares look modestly undervalued, with the Inigo integration the thing to watch.
bull: Home-price equity keeps claims minimal, Inigo diversifies earnings smoothly, and buybacks at a single-digit multiple compound value.
bear: Housing weakens and unemployment rises just as Inigo takes a large catastrophe or casualty loss, hitting both halves of the business at once.
